dossier.public_summary: The 6-day dip is deeper in some TESS sectors than others and odd and even dips differ by a factor of two with a secondary eclipse, while on the rotation period of this spotted star. Together this matches an eclipsing binary or stellar blend at half its true period, not a small planet on the target.

reasons.why: Depth changes wildly between sectors: 801 ppm in sector 27 vs 12 ppm in sector 1 vs 438 ppm in sector 68, a 229.7% change, and sector_depths_by_source verdict is changes_within_a_source even within SPOC 2-min (p_constant 9.969423461572195e-16). A true planet on the target must have consistent depth.

Odd transits are twice as deep as even transits (471.3 ppm vs 239.9 ppm). Sector-level odd/even reaches max 8.337 sigma, classic signature of an eclipsing binary seen at half its true period, not a planet.
Significant secondary eclipse well above best brightening (3.363) indicates a luminous companion, inconsistent with a 1.5 Rearth planet.
Individual transit depths are extremely inconsistent with three shallow dips disappearing in other sectors, arguing the signal is not repeatable transits on the target.

Dip period is essentially the star's rotation period with strong spot modulation, seen in sectors where sector_depths p_constant fails; phase_curve not required but spot variability explains apparent dips.
